title: FLUX.1 Kontext · conditioning
question: What happens to the reference while the output is sampled?
choices: It is denoised with the target.
It is used only after decoding.
explanation: The reference provides context tokens while the target sequence evolves. See Architecture, §3 of the paper.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · time direction
question: With zₜ = (1−t)x + tε, which direction generates an image?
explanation: t = 1 is noise and t = 0 is the clean target. Backward integration explains the minus sign in the toy Euler update.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · velocity
question: For x = 2 and ε = 10, what is the exact training velocity?
explanation: Differentiate (1−t)x + tε with respect to t: ε−x = 8. The sampling update goes backward in time.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · position
question: What does the 1 in reference position (1, h, w) mean?
choices: It identifies the reference separately from target positions.
explanation: The virtual time coordinate separates image sequences. It is distinct from the flow noise time t.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · dev
question: Which statement matches the report’s dev recipe?
choices: LADD with the same joint task training as pro.
Guidance distillation into a 12B transformer, focused on image-to-image.
No model training ever takes place.
explanation: Section 3 distinguishes dev guidance distillation and editing-only training from pro’s flow training followed by LADD.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · metric
question: An editor returns the reference unchanged and gets a high face-similarity score. What follows?
choices: Identity similarity alone cannot establish instruction following.
All image quality metrics must be low.
explanation: An unchanged reference can preserve identity while ignoring the instruction. Evaluate preservation and the requested change together.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · benchmark
question: What does 1,026 refer to in KontextBench?
choices: Image–prompt pairs, derived from 108 base images.
explanation: Section 4.1 reports 1,026 pairs across five categories. Several instructions can reuse a base image.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · multi image
question: What is established about multiple reference images in this report?
choices: They are the focus of every experiment.
They are impossible with sequence concatenation.
The formulation extends to them, but the report focuses on single-reference conditioning.
explanation: An architecture supporting an extension is different from evidence that the extension was trained and evaluated.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · limits
question: How should you describe multi-turn consistency?
choices: Reduced drift in reported comparisons, with failures still documented.
Evidence that distillation cannot cause artifacts.
explanation: Section 5 and Figure 15 show identity degradation, instruction failures, and artifacts after repeated edits.

title: FLUX.1 Kontext · concat
question: Why can sequence concatenation handle different input/output grids?
choices: It makes the images have identical pixels.
It appends separate token sequences rather than pairing channels at each matching location.
explanation: Separate sequences can contain different numbers of spatial tokens. Position embeddings retain their spatial organization.

title: DiffAtlas · joint
question: What does DiffAtlas learn jointly?
choices: Images and their matching mask representations
Only masks conditioned on clean scans
A fixed atlas deformation for each patient
explanation: It denoises image–mask pairs, learning their joint distribution. Inference then uses noisy image replacement to condition generation.

title: DiffAtlas · replacement
question: At inference, what is replaced at each time step?
choices: Both image and mask with fresh noise
Only the image part, with the appropriately noised patient scan
Only the mask, with the annotation
explanation: Image channels are overwritten with the observed scan noised to the current level. The mask state carries progress forward.

title: DiffAtlas · noise
question: Why use a noisy patient scan instead of a clean scan at every step?
choices: To hide the patient from the model
To remove the need for annotated training data
To match the image corruption level expected at the current time
To update the model weights at test time
explanation: Training uses noisy paired states at each time. Replacement should match that corruption level.

title: DiffAtlas · sdf
question: What extra information does a signed distance field give?
choices: Distance to a boundary and which side a location is on
explanation: The field encodes graded geometry rather than just a discrete label. It encourages continuity but does not guarantee correctness.

title: DiffAtlas · number
question: With ᾱ = 0.64, image value 0.8, and noise 0.2, what is the noisy image value?

title: DiffAtlas · loss
question: What does the paper’s training loss compare?
choices: Predicted noise and known added noise, across both image and mask
Only Dice scores from different datasets
explanation: Equation 6 trains noise prediction on the pair. The training loss changes weights; inference replacement changes the current sample state.

title: DiffAtlas · zero
question: What does zero-shot CT-to-MRI evaluation mean here?
choices: The model never sees any training data
MRI ground-truth masks are inserted during sampling
Source CT training is used without target MRI training
The target MRI scan is never shown to the model
explanation: The model has learned from labeled source data. Target scans guide inference, but target-modality training is absent.

title: DiffAtlas · ablation
question: Do the reported baseline comparisons isolate the benefit of the SDF alone?
choices: Yes, any higher Dice proves the SDF caused it
Yes, because all diffusion methods are identical
No; a controlled component ablation is needed
explanation: Several design choices differ. The v1 comparisons support the tested system but do not isolate each component’s causal contribution.

title: REPA · teacher
question: What does the REPA teacher receive during training?
choices: The same clean image corresponding to the noisy latent.
Fresh Gaussian noise unrelated to the example.
explanation: The frozen visual encoder supplies clean-image feature targets while the generator receives a corrupted latent.

title: REPA · gradient
question: Which parameters does the alignment branch directly train?
choices: The projection and generator blocks upstream of its attachment.
Only generator blocks after the attachment.
explanation: Alignment gradients flow through the projection into the early generator; later blocks are trained by the generation loss.

title: REPA · cosine
question: A projected feature is multiplied by a positive factor of 10. What happens to its cosine similarity?
choices: It stays the same, for nonzero vectors.
explanation: Cosine divides the dot product by both vector lengths; a positive scale cancels.

title: REPA · loss
question: Velocity loss is 1, REPA loss is −0.8, and λ is 0.5. What is the combined loss?
explanation: The objective is 1 + 0.5 × (−0.8) = 0.6. Negative cosine is intentionally minimized.

title: REPA · inference
question: What extra REPA networks must be evaluated for each generated image?
choices: The teacher but not the projection.
Neither the teacher nor projection is needed.
explanation: They provide training supervision; sampling retains the trained generator and VAE decoder.

title: REPA · speed
question: What does the 7M / 400K = 17.5 comparison directly establish?
choices: 17.5 times fewer training iterations at better reported unguided FID.
17.5 times lower total compute including teacher pretraining.
explanation: The table compares iteration budgets and FID, not wall-clock time or sampling cost.

title: REPA · depth
question: Depth 16 has better probe accuracy but worse FID than depth 8. What follows?
choices: More semantic probe accuracy need not improve generation quality.
The teacher must run during sampling.
explanation: Table 2 separates two goals: recognition-friendly representations and generation performance.

title: REPA · time
question: For zₜ = (1−t)z + tε, which sampling direction reaches data?
explanation: At t=1 the state is noise; at t=0 it is data. A backward Euler ODE illustration subtracts a positive step times velocity.

title: Mean Flows · curvature
question: Why can generation curve despite straight training pairs?
choices: The marginal velocity averages possible pairs at each state.
Every training pair is secretly curved.
The VAE always rotates each step.
explanation: The changing conditional mean of pair velocities can induce curved marginal ODE trajectories even with exact fields.

title: Mean Flows · interval
question: Why does average velocity depend on destination time r?
choices: Different intervals can have different average velocities.
explanation: Average velocity summarizes a specified interval, so changing its destination changes the quantity being predicted.

title: Mean Flows · jvp
question: Which JVP tangent differentiates u(z, r, t) along the flow with fixed r?
explanation: The state moves with velocity v, destination r stays fixed, and current time increases at unit rate.

title: Mean Flows · detach
question: What does stopping the target gradient accomplish?
choices: It removes the JVP value from the target.
It makes the target identical at every update.
It avoids backpropagating through the target JVP during the weight update.
explanation: The target still uses the derivative and changes across updates; only its gradient contribution is detached.

title: Mean Flows · numbers
question: If v = 4, t − r = 0.5 and JVP = 2, what is the target?
explanation: The MeanFlow target is 4 − 0.5 × 2 = 3.

title: Mean Flows · diagonal
question: What happens to the training target when r = t?
choices: The correction vanishes, giving the Flow Matching target.
The entire loss is always zero.
explanation: The target formula multiplies the derivative by t − r, so diagonal samples use instantaneous velocity supervision.

title: Mean Flows · nfe
question: Why can guided MeanFlow sampling retain 1-NFE?
choices: The unconditional call is not counted.
The model learns the guided average field during training.
VAE decoding performs the second flow call.
explanation: Guidance enters the training target, allowing a single conditional average-velocity prediction at inference. VAE decoding is separate work.

title: Mean Flows · evidence
question: Which statement correctly describes the course Table 2 result of FID 2.20?
choices: It uses 2-NFE with XL/2+ trained for 1,000 epochs.
explanation: The main 240-epoch XL/2 gets 3.43 at 1-NFE and 2.93 at 2-NFE. The 2.20 result also changes training and configuration.

title: DiME · clean
question: Why does DiME roll the noisy state out to a clean image before evaluating the classifier?
choices: The classifier under explanation was trained on clean images.
The classifier weights must change every step.
The DDPM cannot accept noisy images.
The clean image replaces the original reference permanently.
explanation: The clean rollout gives the existing classifier an appropriate input without retraining it.

title: DiME · state
question: What is carried forward between outer sampling steps?
choices: An independently chosen face each time.
explanation: Clean rollouts supply gradients; guided reverse transitions advance the noisy state.

title: DiME · surrogate
question: What does the reciprocal-square-root-alpha factor represent?
choices: An exact Jacobian of every learned reverse chain.
A gradient-transfer approximation motivated by fixed-noise forward corruption.
explanation: The algebraic surrogate has this derivative, but the actual rollout Jacobian need not equal it.

title: DiME · variance
question: With mean 0.70, variance 0.04 and guidance gradient 0.5, what is the shifted mean?
explanation: Subtract variance times gradient: 0.70 − 0.04 × 0.5 = 0.68. Sampling noise is a separate term.

title: DiME · training
question: What changes when DiME explains a single image?
choices: The image state, while classifier and DDPM weights stay fixed.
explanation: Input gradients steer sampling; they are not parameter updates.

title: DiME · cost
question: Why is DiME still expensive despite avoiding rollout backpropagation?
choices: It retrains a DDPM for every explanation.
Clean previews still require many denoiser forward evaluations.
It queries a text model for each pixel.
explanation: Avoiding a deep derivative graph saves memory but leaves repeated clean rollouts; the paper reports about 1,800 DDPM calls.

title: DiME · mnac
question: Why can a lower number of changed attributes be misleading?
choices: Every extra changed attribute is always good.
Additional changes may reveal associations used by the classifier.
explanation: A method may hide correlated attribute changes while obtaining low MNAC; use complementary evidence.

title: DiME · fid
question: Why should Table 1 FID be read together with flip rates?
choices: FID already includes all failures as zero.
Flip rate and FID are identical.
FID proves each explanation is causal.
FID is computed on successful explanations, whose subsets differ by method.
explanation: Success filtering and different sample counts complicate comparisons of image-distribution quality.

title: Qwen-Image · time
question: Under Qwen-Image Equation 1, which time is pure noise?
choices: Time is the reference frame ID.
explanation: The paper uses xₜ = tz + (1−t)ε, so noise is at 0 and data at 1.

title: Qwen-Image · velocity
question: For clean latent 2 and noise 10, what is the flow velocity target?
explanation: Differentiate tz + (1−t)ε: z−ε = 2−10 = −8.

title: Qwen-Image · dual
question: Why encode an editing reference with both Qwen2.5-VL and the VAE?
choices: To generate two independent final images.
To supply semantic understanding and reconstructive appearance information.
To guarantee all unedited pixels are identical.
explanation: The semantic branch helps instruction following; clean VAE tokens help preserve visual detail. Neither is an exact preservation guarantee.

title: Qwen-Image · decoder
question: Which part is adapted in the text-aware VAE training described in §2.3?
choices: The image decoder, with the shared encoder frozen.
explanation: The report fine-tunes the image decoder on text-rich data to improve fine-detail reconstruction.

title: Qwen-Image · positions
question: Does placing text position IDs on a diagonal make output text diagonal?
choices: No; these IDs organize token positions for attention.
Yes, every generated word must follow that diagonal.
Yes, unless noise time is zero.
No, because position encoding is removed during inference.
explanation: MSRoPE encodes text order across both axes. Position IDs do not prescribe rendered word coordinates.

title: Qwen-Image · curriculum
question: What does synthetic text data mean in this report?
choices: Unfiltered outputs from other image generators.
Controlled rendering of text in backgrounds, scenes, and templates.
explanation: Controlled rendering supplies reliable glyph coverage and layout examples; the report distinguishes it from other models’ generated images.

title: Qwen-Image · evidence
question: What does the ChineseWord Level-3 accuracy of 6.48% show?
choices: All Chinese text rendering is solved.
Rare-character rendering remains difficult despite the aggregate lead.
The VAE reconstructs only 6.48% of pixels.
explanation: ChineseWord evaluates single characters grouped into tiers; aggregate superiority does not remove rare-character failures.

title: Qwen-Image · state
question: What changes repeatedly during ordinary editing inference?
choices: The noisy target latent, conditioned on fixed reference features.
explanation: The reference provides conditioning; the generated target state advances along the flow, with model parameters fixed.

title: Generative overview · 2 · Three ways to learn a generator
question: Why can attractive GAN samples still indicate a poor distribution model?
choices: They may cover only a few modes.
The discriminator is always absent in training.
explanation: Mode collapse can omit kinds of examples even when individual samples look convincing.

title: Generative overview · VAE
question: How does the ordinary VAE generation path begin?
choices: Sample a latent from the prior.
explanation: Prior sampling followed by decoding generates without requiring an input example.

title: Generative overview · Training versus sampling
question: What changes during ordinary iterative inference?
choices: The sample state, with weights fixed.
The network weights after each loss.
explanation: Training updates parameters; inference uses those parameters to evolve a sample.

title: Generative overview · Noise targets
question: Why is the target noise known in diffusion training?
explanation: Artificial corruption creates a known supervised target.

title: Generative overview · Flow example
question: With z = 2, x = 6 and y(t) = (1−t)z + tx, what is y(0.5)?
explanation: The midpoint is 0.5×2 + 0.5×6 = 4; the constant pairwise target velocity is also 4.

title: Generative overview · Deterministic sampling
question: Does a deterministic sampler remove all output diversity?
choices: Yes, its output ignores initial noise.
No, different starting noise can give different outputs.
Yes, it must retrieve a stored image.
No, because it must update weights.
explanation: Determinism fixes the trajectory given its inputs, including the initial noise.

title: Generative overview · Representation and context
question: Which distinction separates latent diffusion from conditioning?
choices: Both specify the number of solver steps.
Latent diffusion chooses a representation; conditioning supplies context.
Latent diffusion guarantees exact pixel preservation.
explanation: Compressed representation and context influence are separate design choices.

title: Generative overview · Evidence limits
question: What quantitative conclusion can this reading overview establish?
choices: Flow matching always wins every benchmark.
GANs always sample fastest at equal quality.
None of these: it supplies no controlled benchmark table.
explanation: The overview makes qualitative comparisons; quantitative claims need the underlying papers and a specified protocol.

title: Lecture 2 · Noise prediction
question: During DDPM training, what supplies the noise target?
choices: The known Gaussian noise used to corrupt the training image.
A classifier applied only to clean images.
An unknown target inferred after sampling.
explanation: The training corruption is constructed, so its sampled noise is known. At inference there is no clean training target.

title: Lecture 2 · Reverse SDE versus ODE
question: How does the probability-flow ODE differ from the reverse SDE?
choices: It only sets the random sample to zero.
It removes fresh noise and uses half the score coefficient in its drift.
It reverses the sign of every network weight.
It must use the same trajectories as the SDE.
explanation: For the lecture’s time-only diffusion coefficient, the score coefficient changes from g² to g²/2. Shared ideal marginals do not mean identical trajectories.

title: Lecture 2 · Flow time convention
question: In slide 17’s straight noise-to-data path, x₀ = −2 and x₁ = 2. What velocity target is used?
choices: The current state, whatever its value.
explanation: The derivative of (1−t)x₀ + tx₁ is x₁−x₀ = 4. Here time 0 means noise, unlike the earlier diffusion notation.

title: Lecture 2 · Latent inference
question: Which path describes text-to-image latent generation after training?
choices: Encode an unavailable target image at each step.
Decode Gaussian pixel noise before encoding a prompt.
Run a discriminator instead of the decoder.
Draw latent noise, repeatedly denoise with conditioning, then decode.
explanation: Training uses encoded images, but text-to-image inference has no source image to encode. The final generated latent is decoded.

title: Lecture 2 · Attention arithmetic
question: Attention weights are (1/4, 3/4), with scalar values (2, 6). What is the output?
choices: 6, because attention always selects only the best key.
explanation: Attention forms a weighted sum: (1/4)×2 + (3/4)×6 = 5. It is not generally hard selection of one value.

title: Lecture 2 · Guidance convention
question: For s = sᵤ + γ(s꜀ − sᵤ), what does γ = 1 return?
explanation: Substitution cancels sᵤ and returns s꜀. Values above 1 extrapolate; other guidance conventions can shift the parameter.

title: Lecture 2 · Metric limits
question: Why can Inception Score miss poor within-class diversity?
choices: It compares all generated images to real images pixel by pixel.
It is exactly a coverage measure.
Confident predictions spread across classes can coexist with repeated images within each class.
It directly measures calibrated medical uncertainty.
explanation: IS uses classifier predictions and their generated marginal. It does not compare a real-image reference set or ensure within-class diversity.

title: Lecture 2 · Generation cost
question: What is needed to assess a claimed sampling speed improvement?
choices: Only the number of time steps.
Only whether the sampler is deterministic.
Network evaluations, cost per evaluation, resolution, hardware, and matched quality.
explanation: Step-aware networks, latent generation and fewer-step samplers change different cost factors. The complete generation path matters.

title: Flow Matching · path
question: What does the linear path xₜ = tz + (1−t)ε represent at t = 0?
explanation: The supplied notes use noise-to-data time: t=0 gives ε and t=1 gives z.

title: Flow Matching · target
question: What target does linear-path conditional flow matching regress against?
choices: The displacement z−ε, interpreted as a velocity.
explanation: Differentiating tz+(1−t)ε at a fixed pair gives z−ε. The network receives the mixed state and time.

title: Flow Matching · posterior
question: How are conditional velocities combined into the marginal field at x?
choices: Using posterior endpoint weights given x and t.
explanation: Bayes weights depend on how likely each endpoint is to have produced this noisy state.

title: Flow Matching · loss
question: Can conditional regression loss remain positive when the marginal field is learned perfectly?
choices: Only if time is sampled incorrectly.
Yes: conditional targets can have irreducible variance.
explanation: The conditional loss equals marginal squared error plus a parameter-independent target-variance term.

title: Flow Matching · sampling
question: What does simulation-free mean in flow matching?
choices: Training samples a state and target directly; inference still integrates a field.
The trained network knows the clean endpoint.
explanation: Algorithm 3 does not roll out an ODE during training. The generative ODE still needs numerical integration.

title: Flow Matching · sde
question: What accompanies Brownian noise when extending the flow to an SDE with the same ideal marginals?
choices: A drift correction equal to σₜ² times the score divided by two.
A retraining update after each step.
A reset to the initial sample.
explanation: The score correction cancels the noise-induced spreading in the Fokker–Planck equation, in the exact continuous-time setting.

title: Flow Matching · guidance
question: For CFG = (1−w)u_unconditional + w u_conditional, what does w=1 do?
explanation: w=1 removes the unconditional coefficient. Values above one extrapolate; stronger guidance is a heuristic.

title: Flow Matching · latent
question: Why train a generative flow on autoencoder latents?
choices: The decoder makes any latent valid.
Autoencoder training proves the latents are exactly standard Gaussian.
The encoder is needed to supply the target image at text-to-image inference.
The encoded-data distribution still needs to be modeled.
explanation: Regularizing latents toward a Gaussian does not force the aggregated distribution to equal that Gaussian. The learned flow models encoded data before decoding.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · Autoregressive dependence
question: What does causal masking ensure?
choices: A prediction cannot use future entries.
Sampling all tokens is always parallel.
explanation: A conditional may depend on its prefix; the mask blocks future leakage.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · Flow volume
question: For x = 2z + 1, how does density at corresponding points change?
explanation: The map doubles interval width, so density halves to preserve probability mass.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · VAE generation
question: Which path generates an unconditional observation in the VAE described here?
choices: Prior sample → decoder distribution → observation sample.
explanation: The encoder helps approximate the posterior during training; generation can start from the prior.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · ELBO gap
question: What determines the gap between exact log-likelihood and the ELBO?
choices: KL from the prior to itself.
The number of generated samples alone.
KL from the variational posterior to the true posterior.
explanation: The posterior-to-posterior KL is the nonnegative gap; the encoder-to-prior KL is a different term inside the ELBO.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · Reparameterization
question: With μ = 1, σ = 0.5 and ε = −2, what are z and the encoder variance?
explanation: z = μ + σε = 0, and variance is the square of the standard deviation.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · GAN gradients
question: During a generator update, what does holding discriminator weights fixed mean?
choices: Block all gradients through the discriminator.
Keep its weights fixed but propagate input gradients to the generator.
explanation: The discriminator supplies a differentiable signal while only generator parameters are updated.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · Noise to score
question: For x̃ = x + σε, how is predicted noise converted to a score?
choices: Multiply by σ without changing sign.
explanation: The Gaussian conditional score is −ε/σ; the learned noise prediction uses the same conversion.

title: Deep Generative Modeling · Langevin noise
question: Why is repeatedly following the standard-normal score without noise not Gaussian sampling?
choices: It trains the network too quickly.
It drifts toward the mode instead of maintaining the distribution.
explanation: The deterministic drift contracts toward zero; the properly scaled random term is essential to the Langevin construction.

title: Neural compression · Lossless stage
question: What does a lossless entropy decoder guarantee inside this lossy codec?
choices: The quantized indices are recovered exactly.
The original pixels are recovered exactly.
explanation: Quantization or the learned transform can lose image information before the lossless entropy stage.

title: Neural compression · Training path
question: Why can the chapter train without running an actual entropy coder?
choices: The image is already a bitstream.
A differentiable probability-based rate surrogate enters the loss.
Quantization always has an exact gradient.
explanation: The rate surrogate trains the entropy model and representation; real coding remains necessary for deployment.

title: Neural compression · Quantization tie
question: For y = 0.5 and codebook (0,1), what does the symmetric soft quantizer output as sharpness increases?
choices: The equal mixture 0.5, unless symmetry is broken.
explanation: The similarities tie, so softmax gives equal weights. Hard quantization needs a tie rule and chooses an endpoint.

title: Neural compression · Ideal versus actual bits
question: The worked sequence has ideal information content 1.415 bits. How long is its illustrated binary prefix-code payload?
explanation: The actual code transmits 01. A fractional ideal length is not the size of that finite message.

title: Neural compression · Decode versus sample
question: How does an autoregressive entropy decoder obtain the next index?
choices: It recovers it from bits using the distribution conditioned on the decoded prefix.
explanation: Decoding must reproduce the encoded sequence; sampling instead creates a new sequence.

title: Neural compression · Fixed-width accounting
question: Four indices use a four-entry codebook for a 16-pixel grayscale image. What is fixed-width payload bpp?
explanation: Each index needs log₂4 = 2 bits: 8 bits total divided by 16 pixels is 0.5 bpp, excluding overhead.

title: Neural compression · Rate penalty
question: In distortion + β × rate, what does increasing β favor when comparing fixed candidates?
choices: A change from bits to nats automatically.
explanation: Increasing the multiplier on rate makes bits more expensive; the units and normalization must remain fixed.

title: Neural compression · Evidence limits
question: What does the chapter’s single-β training plot establish about codec comparisons?
choices: Its rate axis is necessarily complete-file bpp.
It illustrates training behavior, without establishing a baseline codec advantage.
explanation: The example lacks baseline and full-stream accounting; a training curve is not a rate–distortion frontier.

title: GANs · signal
question: What does the GAN discriminator estimate in the balanced classification task?
explanation: The scalar distinguishes training-data origin from generator origin, not semantic classes.

title: GANs · freeze
question: During the generator step, what does freezing the discriminator mean?
choices: Keep its weights fixed while differentiating through its input.
Replace its output with one half.
Train it only on real data.
explanation: The chain rule must still connect the discriminator output to generator parameters.

title: GANs · sample
question: What is required for unconditional sampling after training?
choices: A real image and an encoder.
A noise draw and a generator forward pass.
explanation: The original sampling path uses the noise prior and the fixed generator alone.

title: GANs · gradient
question: When the fake score is 0.01, what is the non-saturating loss derivative with respect to its logit?
explanation: For −log sigmoid(a), the derivative is sigmoid(a)−1. This is a logit derivative, not a parameter gradient.

title: GANs · collapse
question: Why does independent input noise not guarantee diverse generated outputs?
choices: G can map many noise values to the same output.
D is needed to inject sampling noise.
The prior must be learned from images.
explanation: A constant or collapsed generator can discard the variation in its inputs.

title: GANs · optimal
question: At a point where data density is 3 and generator density is 1, what is the ideal balanced discriminator score?
explanation: The optimal score is data/(data+generator), so 3/(3+1)=3/4.

title: GANs · theorem
question: Why does the original convergence proof not guarantee practical neural GAN convergence?
choices: It assumes ideal capacity, optimal D and distribution-space updates.
It requires D to stay untrained.
explanation: Finite networks optimize parameters and need not satisfy the proof’s idealized assumptions.

title: GANs · evidence
question: What do the paper’s Table 1 scores measure?
choices: Test log-likelihood under a Parzen estimator fitted to generated samples.
explanation: The fitted estimator and validation-selected kernel width are part of the evaluation; it is not exact model likelihood.
